text: An IT Business Development Executive finds organizations with problems the agency can solve, earns a useful conversation, determines whether a commercial opportunity exists, and helps the buyer and delivery team agree on the next step. In small agencies, the BDE may own prospecting through closure. In larger firms, those responsibilities are divided. Clarify your job boundary before accepting a quota. A request for an app is not yet an opportunity. An opportunity needs a plausible business problem, an identifiable owner, commercial potential, and a credible path to a decision. A meeting with someone who is only collecting prices is a conversation until those conditions improve.

Review commitments first. Resolve overdue follow-ups, customer questions, and blocked approvals. Research a small number of suitable accounts. In one illustrative cohort, 100 suitable accounts produce 12 positive replies, 8 held meetings, 4 qualified opportunities, 3 proposals, and 1 win. Meeting-to-opportunity conversion is 50%. section_title: Why tools do not fix an unclear offer
text: Apollo can find contact records. Clay can combine data and workflows. An email sequencer can schedule messages. None can decide whether the agency has relevant proof, whether a buyer has a problem, or whether delivery can fulfill the promise. Starting with volume creates weak targeting, generic claims, irrelevant meetings, and preventable reputation damage. The prerequisite is a useful answer to four questions: Who can we help? With which expensive or urgent problem? Why should this buyer trust us? What can we deliver profitably now?

Complete this with the sales manager, delivery lead, and finance owner. Treat unknown items as work to do, not permission to guess. Weak: “We do every technology for every industry at affordable prices.” It gives the buyer no useful way to assess fit. Stronger illustrative positioning: “We help field-service operators replace duplicate paper and spreadsheet reporting with an offline-capable reporting workflow connected to billing.” This specifies a buyer, a problem, and a deliverable. Only use it if the agency can show relevant work. Differentiate using evidence: a reusable migration method, accessible design expertise, a domain workflow, a reliable transition plan, or a relevant reference. “Quality,” “innovation,” and “customer focus” become useful only when supported by concrete practices.

Decline or escalate requests involving deceptive claims, unauthorized data access, impossible delivery conditions, payment terms outside policy, or missing specialist capability. Defer when there is no owner, no credible funding route, no access to essential systems, or no reason to change. Record the reason and the condition that would justify reopening. A small budget is not automatically a bad lead. A smaller scope, paid diagnostic, existing product, or referral may fit. A large budget is not automatically a good lead if liabilities and delivery risks are uncontrolled. Foundation gate. Deliver a two-minute company introduction, explain two offers and their exclusions, present one approved case study, classify five accounts, calculate one margin example, and identify three disqualifiers. Manager scores accuracy 30, relevance 25, commercial judgment 25, clarity 20. Pass at 80/100 with no fabricated claims or unauthorized promises. Full-scale lead generation remains locked until this gate and the technical fluency gate in Chapter 22 are passed.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
section_title: Separate what is sold from how it is billed
text: A mobile app is a service deliverable. Fixed price is a pricing model. Staff augmentation is a responsibility model. MVP is a scope strategy. Managed service is an operating commitment. These dimensions can combine. For example, an MVP may begin with fixed-fee discovery and continue with capped monthly time and materials. An agency sells delivery capacity, expertise, risk reduction, or an operated outcome. Revenue must cover direct staff cost, delivery management, rework, tools, overhead, and profit. Utilization means how much available capacity is spent on billable work. A high hourly rate does not ensure profit if the team spends too many unbilled hours. The cards below use the requested commercial format. Example amounts are hypothetical USD training figures, excluding taxes, licenses, cloud charges, and travel unless stated. Complexity is relative: low means bounded and familiar; medium means multiple workflows or dependencies; high means substantial integration, regulatory, migration, or uncertainty risk.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What it is: A finite piece of work with an agreed objective and completion condition. Why businesses buy it and problem solved: A missing portal, workflow, or product blocks operations or revenue. When to sell: There is an owner, a defined outcome, and a path to acceptance. When not to sell: Continuous operational responsibility is being disguised as a one-off build. Who buys and key buyer: Founders and operating departments; budget usually sits with the founder, product head, or IT head. Terminology: Scope, milestone, deliverable, acceptance. Discovery: What must users accomplish? Who accepts completion? Integrations: Existing identity, CRM, payments, or reporting. Typical team: Product analyst, designer, developers, QA, project manager. Complexity: Medium to high. Commercial model: Fixed price or T&M. Example project and pitch: A $30,000 dealer portal. “We can map dealer ordering and deliver the first approved workflow in stages.” Advantage: Clear objective. Risk and objection: Scope expands while price stays fixed; buyer fears delays. Common mistake: Selling a feature list without acceptance criteria.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: One agreed price for defined scope. Why and problem: Buyer needs budget certainty. Sell when: Requirements, dependencies, and acceptance are sufficiently known. Do not sell when: Critical integration or data feasibility remains unresolved. Who and key buyer: Finance-conscious business sponsor with procurement. Terminology: Baseline scope, change request, assumptions, contingency. Discovery: What is excluded? Which client inputs can delay us? Integrations: Validate access and API behavior before committing. Team: Estimating technical lead, delivery team, PM. Complexity: Any size, but uncertainty must be bounded. Commercial model: Milestone payments against explicit deliverables. Example and pitch: $18,000 for three approved workflows after discovery. “We can commit to this scope and price once these dependencies are confirmed.” Advantage: Predictable commercial envelope. Risk: Agency bears estimation risk. Objection: “Why pay for changes?” Explain baseline versus new requirements. Mistake: Giving a fixed quote from a one-paragraph brief.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Charge for approved effort at agreed rates, plus agreed expenses. Why and problem: Priorities evolve or uncertainty cannot be priced sensibly. Sell when: Buyer can govern the backlog and review progress. Do not sell when: Buyer needs a guaranteed total without controlling scope. Buyer: Product head or CTO; finance approves budget. Terms: Burn rate, cap, timesheet, backlog. Questions: Who prioritizes? What spend triggers approval? Integrations: Any, with exploratory work budgeted. Team: Cross-functional delivery team. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Weekly reporting and monthly invoicing, optionally with a spending cap. Example and pitch: Four-week work period capped at $16,000, then review. “You can change priorities while keeping visibility into spend and completed work.” Advantage: Flexibility. Risk: Poor governance creates endless spending. Objection: “Is this a blank cheque?” Offer budget alerts and stop points. Mistake: Treating a cap as a promise to complete every feature.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: A billing unit for small tasks or consulting; often part of T&M. Why and problem: A buyer needs limited expert help. Sell when: Work can be authorized in small batches. Do not sell when: Many dependencies require coordinated project ownership. Buyer: Engineering or IT manager. Terms: Minimum engagement, billable hour, rounding, approval. Questions: Who authorizes tasks? What counts as billable? Integrations: The existing codebase and tools. Team: One specialist with review support. Complexity: Low to medium. Model: Example 20 approved hours at $50, or $1,000. Pitch: “Start with a bounded diagnostic and approve further effort after the findings.” Advantage: Low initial commitment. Risk: Context-switching and coordination reduce efficiency. Objection: “Why does this take ten hours?” Explain investigation, validation, and review. Mistake: Quoting only keyboard time and omitting testing.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: A purchased block of hours consumed against approved work. Why and problem: Recurring small tasks are hard to procure individually. Sell when: Demand is intermittent and the task boundaries are clear. Do not sell when: Buyer expects guaranteed 24/7 response without an SLA. Buyer: IT or marketing operations manager. Terms: Expiry, rollover, response window, consumption report. Questions: Which roles can use the hours? Do unused hours expire? Integrations: Existing sites and platforms. Team: Shared support specialists. Complexity: Low to medium. Model: Example 40 hours for $2,000 with explicit validity and scheduling rules. Pitch: “Reserve a small support budget and see the balance after every task.” Advantage: Simple purchasing. Risk: Disputes about expiry or availability. Objection: “What if we do not use it?” Discuss a smaller bucket or retainer. Mistake: Calling prepaid hours an unlimited support plan.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Named engineering capacity allocated to a client. Why and problem: Roadmap demand exceeds the client's hiring capacity. Sell when: The client has a product owner and work to assign. Do not sell when: Nobody can manage priorities or review output. Buyer: CTO or engineering manager. Terms: Allocation, notice, replacement, overlap hours. Questions: Who manages daily work? How will skills be validated? Integrations: Client repository, tickets, CI/CD. Team: Developer, account support, optional tech lead and QA. Complexity: Depends on product and onboarding. Model: Example $6,000 monthly allocation with defined capacity and holidays. Pitch: “Add verified capacity for the integration backlog, with agreed overlap and a documented transition.” Advantage: Continuity. Risk: Dependency on individuals. Objection: “Will the developer be fully allocated?” Specify it contractually. Mistake: Promising unlimited monthly hours or presenting an unavailable CV.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Specialists join the client's operating team while the client retains delivery direction. Why and problem: Temporary skill gaps or workload spikes. Sell when: Responsibilities and supervision are clear. Do not sell when: Buyer expects the agency to own the entire outcome at a staff-only rate. Buyer: Engineering leader, vendor manager, procurement. Terms: Resource onboarding, access, worker classification, replacement. Questions: Who owns delivery risk? Which systems need access? Integrations: Client tools and security controls. Team: Requested specialists plus account owner. Complexity: Medium, sometimes high in regulated environments. Model: Monthly or hourly capacity. Example and pitch: Two QA engineers for three months. “We can support your release team with tested specialists and defined onboarding.” Advantage: Speed and flexibility. Risk: Poor client direction or employment-related complications. Objection: “We prefer employees.” Compare the temporary need honestly. Mistake: Treating augmentation as a managed project without pricing management.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Ongoing responsibility for a defined service with measured operating commitments. Why and problem: Systems need reliable operation and incident response. Sell when: The agency can staff the support model. Do not sell when: On-call capacity or system visibility is missing. Buyer: CIO or IT operations head. Terms: SLA, service hours, severity, response, restoration, escalation. Questions: Which systems? What business loss follows an outage? Integrations: Monitoring, ticketing, cloud, identity. Team: Service manager, engineers, security and escalation support. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Monthly fee with volume and scope limits. Example and pitch: $4,500 monthly for specified business-hours operations. “We will own monitoring and incident handling within these service boundaries.” Advantage: Predictable recurring work. Risk: Underpriced incident load. Objection: “Is resolution guaranteed?” Distinguish response from restoration targets. Mistake: Selling 24/7 as a slogan without staffing it.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: A recurring fee for agreed access, capacity, or deliverables. Why and problem: Buyer needs continuity without procuring every task. Sell when: A repeatable need exists. Do not sell when: Deliverables and availability are undefined. Buyer: Founder, department head, or IT manager. Terms: Included work, cadence, rollover, notice. Questions: Is the fee for availability, hours, or outputs? Integrations: Existing systems. Team: Depends on retained expertise. Complexity: Low to high. Model: Example $3,000 monthly for defined improvement and review work. Pitch: “We can reserve capacity for the priorities you approve each month.” Advantage: Planning continuity. Risk: Mismatched expectations. Objection: “Why pay in a quiet month?” Explain the reservation or change the model. Mistake: Using retainer and managed service as synonyms.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Expert diagnosis and recommendations, sometimes implementation oversight. Why and problem: Buyer must make a difficult technology or investment decision. Sell when: Independent analysis has value. Do not sell when: Buyer only wants free architecture for a competitive tender. Buyer: CEO, CTO, CIO, or business sponsor. Terms: Assessment, options, roadmap, decision record. Questions: Which decision must this work enable? Who will act on it? Integrations: Read-only access to relevant documentation and systems. Team: Domain consultant and architect. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Fixed-fee assessment or expert-day billing. Example and pitch: $5,000 modernization assessment. “You will receive options, risks, and a costed next-step recommendation.” Advantage: Reduces uncertainty. Risk: Advice is never implemented. Objection: “Can you include this free?” Separate light qualification from substantive consulting. Mistake: Delivering a generic slide deck without a decision.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
section_title: Paid discovery and proof of concept
text: What: Discovery defines the problem and scope; a POC tests a specific uncertainty. Why and problem: Buyer should not fund a full build before feasibility is clear. Sell when: Unknowns materially affect viability. Do not sell when: The experiment has no success or stop criteria. Buyer: Product sponsor and CTO. Terms: Hypothesis, test set, feasibility, go/no-go. Questions: What must we learn? What would make us stop? Integrations: Sandbox or representative data. Team: Analyst, architect, targeted engineer, QA. Complexity: Bounded experiment despite potentially complex subject. Model: Example $4,000 fixed-fee assessment. Pitch: “Test the difficult integration first, then decide whether to invest.” Advantage: Limits downside. Risk: Prototype mistaken for production. Objection: “Why not just build?” Explain the cost of the unresolved risk. Mistake: Promising a POC automatically proves scale, security, and reliability.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: The smallest usable product that tests an important commercial assumption. Why and problem: A founder needs evidence before funding a full roadmap. Sell when: There is a target user and testable value proposition. Do not sell when: 'MVP' means a large product at a small price. Buyer: Founder or product leader. Terms: Core journey, hypothesis, activation, learning metric. Questions: What must users do? What result would change the investment decision? Integrations: Only those essential to the core journey. Team: Product lead, designer, full-stack engineer, QA. Complexity: Medium, rising with payments or regulated data. Model: Paid discovery then phased fixed scope or T&M. Example and pitch: $24,000 first release for one buyer group. “Validate one complete workflow before expanding.” Advantage: Focused learning. Risk: Cutting necessary security to save money. Objection: “Can we add five more modules?” Revisit the hypothesis. Mistake: Treating minimum as unreliable.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Continuous improvement of a software product across releases. Why and problem: Customer needs, competition, and operational demands keep changing. Sell when: A product owner can prioritize outcomes. Do not sell when: No funding or ownership exists beyond launch. Buyer: Head of Product or CTO. Terms: Roadmap, backlog, release, technical debt. Questions: Which user behavior or business metric must improve? Integrations: Analytics, support, billing, business systems. Team: Durable product squad. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Monthly T&M squad or capacity agreement. Example and pitch: Three-month enhancement program with monthly reviews. “We will prioritize releases against adoption and operating needs.” Advantage: Compounding domain knowledge. Risk: Feature output replaces value measurement. Objection: “How do we control spend?” Use capacity, outcome reviews, and stop points. Mistake: Selling a roadmap as a fixed list of guaranteed future features.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Fix defects, update dependencies, and support agreed production behavior. Why and problem: Software degrades as environments and threats change. Sell when: Ownership, access, and support hours are known. Do not sell when: The inherited system is unassessed but unlimited responsibility is demanded. Buyer: IT manager or product owner. Terms: Warranty, severity, patch, end of support. Questions: What qualifies as a bug versus enhancement? Integrations: Repository, monitoring, ticketing, hosting. Team: Support engineer, developer, QA. Complexity: Depends on system condition. Model: Assessment plus retainer or ticket- based work. Example and pitch: $1,800 monthly bounded support. “Keep the existing system reliable with a clear queue and escalation path.” Advantage: Continuity. Risk: Legacy defects consume the fee. Objection: “Shouldn't all fixes be free?” Refer to agreed warranty boundaries. Mistake: Including new features in an undefined warranty.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: External testing capability or responsibility for an agreed quality scope. Why and problem: Releases fail, regression takes too long, or internal QA is thin. Sell when: Access, environments, and release ownership are available. Do not sell when: Buyer expects zero defects from a limited test budget. Buyer: Engineering manager or QA head. Terms: Coverage, regression, flaky test, defect severity. Questions: Which failures hurt customers most? Integrations: CI/CD, issue tracker, test data. Team: QA lead, manual or automation engineers. Complexity: Medium. Model: Diagnostic followed by project, capacity, or retainer. Example and pitch: Automate 20 critical checkout tests after a testability review. “Protect the release journeys that create the most business risk.” Advantage: Independent scrutiny. Risk: Brittle automation. Objection: “Developers already test.” Identify uncovered risks. Mistake: Selling test count instead of meaningful coverage.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Improve deployment, infrastructure, reliability, or cloud economics. Why and problem: Releases are slow, outages recur, or costs are unclear. Sell when: Baselines and access can be established. Do not sell when: An infrastructure redesign has no business justification. Buyer: CTO, platform lead, or CIO. Terms: CI/CD, infrastructure as code, RTO, RPO, observability. Questions: What fails today? What does recovery require? Integrations: Cloud, repositories, monitoring, identity. Team: Cloud architect, DevOps or SRE, security. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Assessment, migration project, then optional managed service. Example and pitch: $7,500 deployment and recovery improvement phase. “Make releases repeatable and test recovery before promising uptime.” Advantage: Reduces operating friction. Risk: Migration downtime and uncontrolled spend. Objection: “Cloud is already managed.” Explain customer responsibilities. Mistake: Guaranteeing savings before reviewing usage.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Select, test, integrate, and govern AI for a real workflow. Why and problem: Repetitive language, prediction, image, or speech tasks consume capacity. Sell when: Value, data rights, evaluation, and exception ownership are feasible. Do not sell when: A simple rule solves the problem or errors cannot be controlled. Buyer: Operations head, product leader, CTO. Terms: Evaluation, RAG, inference cost, human review. Questions: Which task? What is an unacceptable error? Integrations: Knowledge stores, CRM, helpdesk, identity. Team: Domain owner, AI engineer, backend engineer, QA, security. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Paid diagnostic and pilot, then phased rollout. Example and pitch: Test an internal support assistant on approved documents. “Measure answer quality and total handling cost before expanding.” Advantage: Potential capacity improvement. Risk: Hallucinations, leakage, cost growth. Objection: “Why not use a chatbot subscription?” Compare workflow integration needs. Mistake: Selling an autonomous agent before proving a supervised workflow.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Coordinated changes to processes, data, systems, and operating behavior. Why and problem: Fragmented workflows limit business performance. Sell when: Leadership will own process change and adoption. Do not sell when: A website redesign is being inflated into enterprise transformation. Buyer: CEO, COO, CIO. Terms: Current state, target state, operating model, adoption. Questions: Which business process and owner? How will behavior change? Integrations: ERP, CRM, finance, operations. Team: Business consultant, architect, change lead, delivery specialists. Complexity: High. Model: Assessment and staged program. Example and pitch: Digitize order-to-cash in phases. “Start with the slowest handoff and measure its effect before wider change.” Advantage: Systemic improvement. Risk: Organizational resistance. Objection: “We cannot disrupt operations.” Design staged transition. Mistake: Pricing software only while omitting training, data cleanup, and adoption.

chapter_title: How IT services businesses make money
text: What: Improve or replace legacy components while preserving needed business behavior. Why and problem: Unsupported systems, slow releases, or fragile integrations raise risk. Sell when: Constraints and migration paths can be assessed. Do not sell when: A functioning system is being rewritten only for fashion. Buyer: CIO, CTO, application owner. Terms: Refactor, replatform, rehost, strangler pattern, rollback. Questions: What must remain stable? Which dependencies are undocumented? Integrations: Legacy databases, jobs, ERP, identity. Team: Architect, legacy and target-stack engineers, QA, migration lead. Complexity: High. Model: Paid assessment then phased T&M or bounded migrations. Example and pitch: Replace one reporting module before the core system. “Reduce the highest-risk dependency without a big-bang rewrite.” Advantage: Controlled risk reduction. Risk: Hidden behavior and data loss. Objection: “Why not replace everything?” Compare operational risk. Mistake: Estimating only new code and forgetting parity testing. Assignment. Choose a model for five requests: unclear AI concept, stable portal scope, temporary QA gap, production support, and legacy migration.

section_title: From problem to an operated system
text: Software work moves from understanding a problem to designing, building, checking, releasing, and improving a system. The sequence is not rigid. Teams revisit requirements and design as they learn. Agile means short learning and delivery cycles with prioritization; it does not mean no documentation, no estimates, or unlimited changes. A sprint is a short planning and delivery period. A backlog is a prioritized list of work. A release is a version made available to users. The definition of done describes the checks required before work counts as complete. A demo shows progress; it is not automatically contractual acceptance.

Business problem: a distributor takes too long to approve credit orders. Business requirement: reduce approval handling time while preserving finance controls. Functional requirement: orders above a configured credit threshold require finance approval before release. User story: “As a finance approver, I need to review flagged orders so that the warehouse releases only authorized credit orders.” Acceptance criteria: An over-limit order enters Pending Approval. Only the finance approver role can approve it. Approval records user, time, and decision. Rejected orders cannot be released. If the finance service is unavailable, the order remains pending and the user sees a retry-safe message. Notification failure must not approve the order. Non-functional requirement: under a defined test load of 100 concurrent users, 95% of approval-list requests complete within two seconds in the agreed environment. This is a sample requirement to validate, not a default promise. The first request sounded like “add an approval button.” Discovery revealed roles, data rules, audit history, integrations, error handling, and performance. Those details explain effort without hiding behind jargon.

The client sponsor owns business priorities and acceptance authority. The product owner clarifies daily requirements. The architect validates technical choices. Engineers and QA estimate their work. BI, or business intelligence, helps people analyze business performance. A warehouse structures analytical data; a lake stores varied data for different uses.

Real- time analytics processes data with low delay and typically costs more to operate than periodic reporting. Ask whether hourly or daily freshness is sufficient.

What: Reduce risks to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Why and problem: Systems and data face misuse, loss, and interruption. Sell when: The scope and authorization are explicit and qualified specialists are available. Do not sell when: The agency lacks the expertise or permission to test. Buyer: CISO, CIO, IT/security head. Terms: Identity, access management, vulnerability, threat, penetration test, remediation. Questions: What assets and data? What authorized scope? Who fixes findings? Integrations: Identity, logging, cloud, code pipelines. Team: Security specialist and remediation owners. Complexity: Medium to high. Model: Scoped assessment and remediation; ongoing service only with capacity. Example and pitch: “Identify and prioritize exposed application risks, then verify the fixes.” Objection: “Will this certify us?” Explain the engagement's limits. Mistake: Equating a scan with a penetration test or compliance certification. Application security concerns software behavior. Cloud security includes configuration and operating controls. Identity and access management decide who can do what. Vulnerability assessment identifies potential weaknesses.

text: Each tree starts with a business request, then branches on a material constraint. Low complexity means limited workflows with known dependencies. Medium includes several roles or integrations. High includes major migration, uncertain devices, sensitive operations, or strong regulatory constraints. These are discussion labels, not estimates. section_title: Learn the workflow and the money
text: Industry fluency begins with how work moves, who pays, what can fail, and which records matter. Use the cards below to form hypotheses, not diagnose a prospect from its sector label. The opportunities are practical ideas to validate, not claims that every company currently wants them. For every sector, ask the operating team to walk through a recent real transaction. Identify the trigger, handoffs, systems, exceptions, approvals, and final result. This reveals more than asking, “Do you need an app?”

Basics and buyers: Providers deliver care while administrators coordinate appointments, records, billing, and patient communication. Buyers include practice owners, operations heads, CIOs, and clinical leaders. Business and technology problems: Administrative burden, missed handoffs, fragmented records, weak interoperability. Typical software and integrations: EHR, scheduling, patient portals, billing; identity, labs, payment and HL7/FHIR interfaces where available. Opportunity and concerns: Patient intake or administrative portals can help, but health data, access, audit, consent, and jurisdiction matter. HIPAA applicability depends on entity, activity, and data, not the word “healthcare.” Relevant business-associate arrangements must be reviewed. [17] Discovery: What data will the portal hold? Which EHR supports access? Who validates workflow safety? Pitch: “Start with intake and appointment communication, with the data and integration boundaries approved first.”

Basics and buyers: Technology supports payments, lending, investments, or related financial activity. Founders, product heads, compliance, and CTOs participate. Problems: Failed transactions, slow onboarding, reconciliation gaps, fraud, disconnected providers. Software and integrations: Payment orchestration, onboarding, ledgers, risk tools; banking, identity/KYC providers, payment gateways. Opportunity and concerns: Reconciliation automation and controlled operational dashboards may be valuable. Funds flow, licensing, payment security, AML/KYC, and data obligations need specialist review. Discovery: Who holds funds? Which party is regulated? What happens on a duplicated or reversed transaction? Pitch: “Map the transaction and reconciliation flow before selecting the integration design.” Do not equate a payment API integration with permission to operate a financial business.

Basics and buyers: Banks manage deposits, lending, payments, and risk under substantial oversight. Buyers include CIOs, business heads, enterprise architects, and vendor-risk teams. Problems: Legacy dependencies, slow releases, complex approvals, inconsistent data. Software and integrations: Core banking, customer channels, risk and reporting; identity, payment rails, enterprise messaging. Opportunity and concerns: Peripheral workflow modernization can be more feasible than replacing the core. Security, resilience, audit, third-party risk, and jurisdiction-specific outsourcing rules matter. Discovery: Which system is authoritative? What change windows and vendor gates apply? Pitch: “Assess one bounded customer-service workflow and its integration risk before proposing broader modernization.” Enterprise readiness and reference requirements may disqualify a young agency from direct core-system work.

Basics and buyers: Insurers price risk, issue policies, collect premiums, and process claims. Buyers include claims operations, CIOs, underwriting, and digital product teams. Problems: Document-heavy claims, duplicate entry, fragmented policy data, slow status updates. Software and integrations: Policy administration, claims systems, document management, broker portals; identity, payments, external data. Opportunity and concerns: Supervised document extraction and claims status workflows. Privacy, auditability, fairness, retention, and decision authority require care. Discovery: Which claim stages need human judgment? What error could wrongly affect a claimant? Pitch: “Reduce document preparation effort while retaining authorized review for claims decisions.” Avoid promising autonomous coverage or payout decisions from a simple AI pilot.

Basics and buyers: Property firms acquire, market, lease, sell, or manage assets. Buyers include owners, sales heads, property operations, and IT. Problems: Lead leakage, repeated listing updates, maintenance coordination, scattered documents. Software and integrations: CRM, listing portals, property management, tenant apps; listing feeds, payments, calendars, accounting. Opportunity and concerns: Lead-to-viewing automation or tenant-service workflows. Personal data, location details, tenancy records, and local transaction rules matter. Discovery: Where do leads enter? Which system owns listing availability? Who follows up? Pitch: “Connect inquiry capture to viewing and follow-up so the team can see where opportunities stall.” A new website will not fix unowned lead response.

Basics and buyers: Projects coordinate contractors, site activity, materials, cost, and compliance evidence. Buyers include contractors, project directors, operations, and finance. Problems: Delayed field reports, missing evidence, change-order disputes, disconnected job costing. Software and integrations: Field reporting, project management, document control; accounting, scheduling, maps, storage. Opportunity and concerns: Offline site reports with photo evidence and approval workflows. Worker data, access, contractual records, and site safety context matter. Discovery: What happens without connectivity? Who signs off quantities and changes? Pitch: “Capture site evidence once and connect approved reports to project and billing workflows.” Do not promise a reporting app replaces engineering or safety approval.

Basics and buyers: Plants transform materials into products while managing quality, capacity, and downtime. Buyers include plant heads, operations, quality, and IT/OT teams. Problems: Manual production logs, unplanned stops, quality traceability gaps. Software and integrations: ERP, MES, maintenance, quality systems; machine data, scanners, PLC/SCADA interfaces where authorized. Opportunity and concerns: Production visibility or digital quality checks at one line. Operational technology segmentation, safety, access, and downtime constraints matter. Discovery: Which machines expose data safely? What is the cost of a stopped line? Pitch: “Pilot visibility on one production line without disturbing machine control.” Never estimate a factory rollout from a dashboard mockup alone.

Basics and buyers: Operators move goods through dispatch, transit, and delivery. Buyers include fleet owners, dispatch heads, COO, and IT. Problems: Late status updates, driver calls, missing proof of delivery, billing delays. Software and integrations: TMS, dispatch, driver apps, tracking; GPS/telematics, maps, customer systems, accounting. Opportunity and concerns: Driver workflow and exception alerts. Location privacy, device access, offline operation, and data accuracy matter. Discovery: Do vehicles already have tracking devices? Which exceptions require action? Pitch: “Connect delivery evidence and exceptions to dispatch so the team can act without repeated calls.” Tracking dots alone may not improve operations.

Basics and buyers: Coordinate suppliers, purchasing, inventory, and fulfillment across organizations. Buyers include supply-chain heads, procurement, operations, and CFOs. Problems: Stock uncertainty, supplier delays, poor forecasts, inconsistent item records. Software and integrations: ERP, WMS, supplier portals, planning tools; EDI, carrier, procurement, and inventory systems. Opportunity and concerns: Supplier visibility or inventory-data reconciliation. Commercial confidentiality, partner access, and source-data ownership matter. Discovery: Which inventory number is trusted? How are exceptions escalated? Pitch: “Create a shared view of purchase and stock exceptions with clear ownership.” Forecasting should follow data validation, not substitute for it.

Basics and buyers: Stores sell inventory and serve customers across physical and digital channels. Buyers include owners, retail operations, merchandising, and IT. Problems: Stock mismatch, disconnected customer data, slow replenishment, inconsistent reporting. Software and integrations: POS, inventory, loyalty, workforce, analytics; accounting, eCommerce, payments. Opportunity and concerns: Store-to-online inventory sync or operating dashboards. Payment security, customer privacy, refunds, and store downtime matter. Discovery: How quickly must stock update? What happens during connectivity loss? Pitch: “Reduce stock discrepancies between stores and online channels with reconciliation and exception handling.” Integration is often more valuable than replacing every system. 7.12 eCommerce Basics and buyers: Online sellers acquire customers, convert orders, fulfill, and manage returns. Buyers include founders, eCommerce heads, operations, and marketing. Problems: Checkout friction, failed orders, fulfillment gaps, poor catalog quality. Software and integrations: Commerce platform, PIM, order management; gateways, shipping, ERP, CRM, analytics.

d orders, fulfillment gaps, poor catalog quality. Software and integrations: Commerce platform, PIM, order management; gateways, shipping, ERP, CRM, analytics.  Opportunity and concerns: Checkout diagnosis, order workflow automation, integration repair. Payment scope, privacy, fraud, tax, and accessibility need review. Discovery: Where does conversion drop? Are abandoned checkouts caused by UX, payment failure, or shipping cost? Pitch: “Diagnose the highest-loss checkout step before proposing a redesign.” Do not promise a conversion uplift without baseline and measurement design.

Basics and buyers: Institutions and training businesses deliver learning and manage learners. Buyers include institution leaders, academic operations, product heads, and IT. Problems: Disconnected enrollment, scheduling, assessment, and learner support. Software and integrations: LMS, student information, assessment tools; identity, payments, video, content systems. Opportunity and concerns: Enrollment workflow or learner-support tools. Student privacy, minors, accessibility, content rights, and assessment integrity matter. Discovery: Who is the learner and who pays? What can an automated assistant answer? Pitch: “Reduce enrollment administration and make the next learner action clear.” Clinical or high-stakes certification assessments require more control than general course content.

Basics and buyers: Sell ongoing access to software and depend on adoption, retention, and expansion. Buyers include founders, CTOs, product and engineering leaders. Problems: Backlog, onboarding friction, reliability, integration demand, technical debt. Software and integrations: The product itself, billing, support, analytics; SSO, CRM, payment, data tools. Opportunity and concerns: A narrow product squad, quality improvement, or enterprise readiness. Tenant isolation, contracts, uptime commitments, data export, and usage economics matter. Discovery: Which roadmap item blocks adoption or a real sale? Pitch: “Address the specific integration or reliability gap that is delaying customer value.” Distinguish a prospect's requested feature from a validated market need.

Basics and buyers: Create, manage, distribute, and monetize content. Buyers include publishers, product heads, content operations, and technology leaders. Problems: Fragmented content workflows, slow publishing, rights confusion, poor distribution. Software and integrations: CMS, digital asset management, streaming, subscriptions; ad platforms, CDN, identity, payments. Opportunity and concerns: Editorial workflow automation or content operations search. Copyright, permissions, provenance, audience privacy, and moderation matter. Discovery: Who owns rights for each content type? Which review must remain human? Pitch: “Reduce publishing handoffs while preserving editorial approval and rights checks.” AI-generated content does not eliminate rights or accuracy review.

Basics and buyers: Sell and coordinate bookings across suppliers. Buyers include travel operators, product, reservations, and IT. Problems: Fragmented inventory, booking failures, slow changes, manual reconciliation. Software and integrations: Booking engines, reservation systems, traveler portals; supplier APIs, GDS where relevant, payments, messaging. Opportunity and concerns: Booking-management workflows or exception handling. Personal and travel-document data, payment, cancellation, and supplier terms matter. Discovery: Is inventory live? What happens if payment succeeds but supplier confirmation fails? Pitch: “Design booking and refund reconciliation around real supplier failure cases.” A search screen is only a small part of a booking system.

Basics and buyers: Hotels and hospitality operators manage rooms, guests, services, and occupancy. Buyers include owners, general managers, operations, and IT. Problems: Repeated guest requests, fragmented property data, manual staff coordination. Software and integrations: Property management, reservations, POS, guest apps; channel managers, payments, messaging. Opportunity and concerns: Staff task management or bounded guest-service assistance. Guest privacy, identity information, multilingual accuracy, and after-hours escalation matter. Discovery: Which requests need a staff member? What systems can confirm availability? Pitch: “Route guest requests to the right staff with status tracking and escalation.” Do not let an AI assistant invent room availability or pricing.

Basics and buyers: Includes manufacturers, dealers, workshops, fleets, and parts businesses. Buyers vary by segment: operations, service, product, engineering, or IT. Problems: Service scheduling, parts visibility, dealer data, inspection records. Software and integrations: Dealer management, workshop systems, connected services; inventory, diagnostic systems, telematics, finance. Opportunity and concerns: Service workflow or inspection evidence. Vehicle/customer data, safety boundaries, device access, and ownership matter. Discovery: Is the system administrative or controlling vehicle behavior? Pitch: “Improve the service booking and inspection handoff while preserving the existing dealer system.” Vehicle control and safety-related software require specialist assurance beyond ordinary app development.

Basics and buyers: Farms and agribusinesses manage land, inputs, equipment, labor, yield, and selling. Buyers include farm owners, cooperatives, agribusiness operations, and product firms. Problems: Scattered records, poor stock visibility, missed tasks, weak cost tracking. Software and integrations: Farm management, field records, finance, equipment dashboards; weather, maps, sensors, accounting. Opportunity and concerns: Offline field task and resource tracking. Connectivity, shared devices, location data, seasonal timing, and data ownership matter. Discovery: Who enters records and when? Does the workflow work without mobile coverage? Pitch: “Start with field tasks and input records that the team can maintain during the season.” Avoid yield promises without agronomic evidence.

Basics and buyers: Agencies deliver public services under public accountability and procurement rules. Buyers include program owners, CIOs, procurement, and security teams. Problems: Paper workflows, inaccessible services, legacy records, slow case handling. Software and integrations: Citizen portals, case management, records; identity, payments, registries, inter-agency systems. Opportunity and concerns: A bounded service workflow or modernization subcontract. Tender eligibility, accessibility, retention, public records, hosting, and security obligations matter. Discovery: What procurement route and accreditation are required? Pitch: “Map one citizen-service journey and the evidence needed for procurement and delivery.” A good conversation is not permission to bypass a tender process.

Basics and buyers: Legal teams manage matters, documents, deadlines, and advice. Buyers include partners, legal operations, general counsel, and IT. Problems: Document search, repeated intake, manual matter updates, billing friction. Software and integrations: Matter management, document systems, time/billing; email, identity, finance, e-signature. Opportunity and concerns: Matter intake or permission-aware search with attorney review. Confidentiality, privilege, access, retention, and source accuracy matter. Discovery: Which documents may be accessed by each matter team? Who checks output? Pitch: “Reduce document-finding time while preserving matter-level permissions and legal review.” Do not sell automated legal conclusions as ordinary chatbot output.

Basics and buyers: Consultancies, agencies, and advisory firms sell expertise and delivery capacity. Buyers include founders, partners, COO, and finance. Problems: Fragmented sales-to-delivery handoffs, resource planning, timesheets, billing, knowledge access. Software and integrations: CRM, PSA, projects, finance, knowledge systems; calendar, documents, accounting. Opportunity and concerns: A connected proposal-to-project workflow or internal knowledge assistant. Client confidentiality, contractual access, utilization economics, and data ownership matter. Discovery: Where is work re-entered? Which handoff delays billing? Pitch: “Connect signed scope, staffing, and billing records so project teams start with the same information.” Avoid assuming every small firm needs a custom platform.

US and Canadian buyers are not interchangeable, especially for outreach rules. UK and European requirements vary by country and recipient type. The Middle East is not one jurisdiction: distinguish the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and other markets, then check hosting, procurement, and language needs. Australia has its own outreach and privacy rules. India-based delivery teams must also plan time-zone overlap, local holidays, tax/payment handling, and cross-border data access. For every deal record buyer location, contracting entity, end-user locations, data locations, invoicing currency, working overlap, and required local partners. Never infer preferences from nationality. Ask about the buyer's actual operating needs. Industry assignment. Choose two sectors the agency can credibly serve. For each, map one workflow, five buyer terms, three integrations, two risk issues, and one approved proof asset. Pass when a domain colleague confirms the workflow and no unverified regulatory promise appears.

An ideal customer profile describes organizations worth pursuing. A buyer persona describes a role within those organizations. A 70-person distributor may fit the ICP; its finance manager, operations head, and IT manager have different priorities. Finding a CTO's email does not establish account fit. Build the ICP from profitable delivery and real wins, not only the founder's preferred industry. Include company type, region, operating problem, relevant systems, trigger, buying capacity, proof fit, and exclusions. Employee count is a rough filter, not a budget estimate.

Identify the user, champion, economic buyer, technical evaluator, security/legal reviewer, procurement owner, and signer. One person may hold several roles. A champion actively helps you navigate the organization and build the case; friendliness alone does not establish a champion. Ask: “Who else needs to be comfortable before this can move forward?” Then: “What would each person need to see?” Record evidence, not just names. Access to the CEO does not bypass security or procurement. Exercise. Map a patient-portal purchase across operations, clinical, IT/security, finance, and procurement. Write one value statement for each. Pass when the statements use each role's priorities and do not repeat the same pitch five times.

Lead generation starts after foundations, technology fluency, and message review. A trainee may research and roleplay before passing; that is not permission for mass outreach. Begin with a small, manager-reviewed campaign in one ICP and one offer. Expand only when fit, message relevance, deliverability, and opportunity quality are credible. Gartner's 2025 release reports that many surveyed B2B buyers prefer self-service for general information, while seeking seller input for contextual fit. Irrelevant outreach can actively damage supplier consideration. This supports useful, specific contact rather than sending a capability brochure to everyone. [5]

This is an operational screening guide, not a complete legal review. Management should approve a country-and-channel playbook before campaigns. Applicable rules may depend on recipient location, sender location, recipient type, data source, and channel. Calling, texts, social messages, and recordings may have different rules from email. Market Rule to build into the campaign process United States CAN-SPAM applies to commercial B2B email too. Use accurate identity and subjects, clear commercial identification, a valid postal address, working opt-out, and timely suppression. Other privacy and calling rules may also apply. [18] Canada CASL generally requires consent or a valid applicable basis/exception for commercial electronic messages, plus identification and unsubscribe requirements. A publicly visible email is not blanket permission. Retain evidence. [19] United Kingdom PECR distinguishes corporate subscribers from individuals such as sole traders. Do not create fake engagement, deceptive reply threads, or mailbox networks to evade restrictions. LinkedIn prohibits unauthorized tools that scrape or automate activity on its site. Use a time budget. Spend more only when account value and evidence justify it. Research should produce a testable reason to talk, not a dossier with irrelevant personal details. 1. Minutes 0 to 3: Read the official homepage, product/service pages, and customer description. Write how the company earns revenue and whom it serves. 2. Minutes 3 to 6: Identify locations, approximate size, leadership, and the likely process owner. Record dates and sources. Separate official facts from directory estimates. 3. section_title: Write about a problem the buyer can recognize
text: Service-first: “We are a leading company offering React, AI, blockchain, cloud, and mobile development. Please share your requirements.” This asks the buyer to perform the diagnosis. Problem-first: “Your rollout announcement mentions three new service regions. How will field teams submit completion evidence when connectivity is poor?” This is useful only when the announcement is real and the question fits the business. A good message contains a verified observation, a cautious problem hypothesis, a relevant reason you might help, and one small next step. Use actual proof or omit the claim. Never invent results, shared connections, case studies, or previous conversations.

The eight sequences below are complete first-contact, follow-up, and close-the-loop paths. Use day 1, day 4, and day 9 as an illustrative cadence in the recipient's working week, not a universal best practice. Stop on reply, refusal, unsubscribe, wrong-person notice, or evidence that contact is inappropriate. For a “later” reply, agree a date or trigger instead of continuing the sequence. Replace every bracket with verified context. If a trigger is absent, ask a neutral question rather than inventing one. Each email must include the sender's real name, agency, valid postal address, and the approved market-specific commercial/opt-out wording. A sample plain footer is: “Business introduction from [Agency], [postal address]. If this is not relevant, reply ‘no’ and I will stop contacting you.” Use an unsubscribe mechanism where required by the campaign and provider rules. This footer does not replace consent where consent is required. Sequence 1 Software development Day 1. Your point about [detail] made me wonder how you handle [relevant workflow]. Is that something your team is working on now?” Acceptance is not consent to an aggressive pitch sequence. Cold call opening: “Hi [Name], this is [Name] from [Agency]. This is a business development call. May I take 20 seconds to explain why I called?” If yes: “I saw [verified trigger]. We work on [relevant problem]. Is [hypothesis] relevant to your team, or have I misunderstood?” If no, stop respectfully. If the caller reaches the wrong person: “Thanks for clarifying. Which function owns that process?” Do not pressure someone for private contact details. Verify any suggested role before contacting. Referral request: “You mentioned [person/team] is reviewing [problem]. If you think our experience is relevant, would you be comfortable introducing us?

I can send a short factual note for you to use.” Obtain the introducer's permission before using their name. Post-event follow-up: “We spoke at [event] about [actual topic]. You mentioned [problem]. Test one material variable at a time, such as persona or problem hypothesis. Keep source quality and channel conditions reasonably consistent. Small samples produce unstable percentages. Record positive replies, held meetings, accepted opportunities, and reasons for rejection. Do not optimize for provocative replies that never become suitable work. Assignment. Write one sequence for a real, approved offer. Annotate every claim with its source. Roleplay three responses: interested, wrong person, and not now. Pass when you stop appropriately and move an interested buyer toward discovery without promising a solution.

Discovery establishes whether a problem is real, worth solving, and suitable for the agency. The buyer should leave with a clearer understanding of the decision. The seller should leave with evidence, open questions, and an agreed next step. A call can succeed by deciding not to proceed. Do not conduct discovery as a questionnaire recital. Follow the buyer's story while checking the necessary areas. Ask one question at a time, listen, summarize, and then go deeper. A useful question often begins with the buyer's last answer.

Read the research sheet, previous messages, and meeting purpose. Confirm attendee roles and the buyer's time zone. Select a relevant case study only if its claims are approved. Prepare a problem hypothesis, three key unknowns, and a possible next step. Ask the technical mentor which signals require escalation. Prepare a shared note with sections for confirmed facts, assumptions, decisions, risks, and actions. If recording is proposed, follow applicable law and company policy, explain the purpose, and obtain the required permission. Do not add recording or transcription bots silently. Send a simple agenda: “Understand the current process, the impact of the problem, and the constraints; decide whether a technical scoping session would be useful.” If the buyer only wants a price, explain which facts are needed to provide a meaningful range.

Time Objective Example wording and required evidence 0 to 3 minutes Agree purpose and time “What would make this conversation useful for you?” Confirm desired outcome. 3 to 8 Understand the business and trigger “What changed that made this worth discussing now?” Identify the process and owner. 8 to 15 Explore the problem and impact “Walk me through the last time this happened.” Capture frequency, consequences, and baseline. 15 to 20 Understand current systems and constraints “Which systems and teams are involved?” Identify data, integration, security, and delivery dependencies. 20 to 25 Establish commercial and decision context “How will you decide whether this is worth funding?” Explore budget route, stakeholders, timing, and alternatives. 25 to 28 Summarize and test understanding “I heard these priorities and these unknowns. What have I missed?” Correct the record. Time Objective Example wording and required evidence 28 to 30 Agree a useful next step Name deliverable, owner, attendees, date, and decision that the next step enables. If a serious issue emerges, adapt the agenda. Do not rush past a security blocker to finish every question.

Business and problem “What does this part of the business do?” prevents assuming the workflow. “Who experiences the problem?” identifies the user. “Show me a recent example” turns vague frustration into evidence. “What did the team do next?” reveals hidden work. “How often does it happen?” establishes volume. “What is the consequence?” connects the task to money, time, risk, or customer experience. If the buyer says, “Our reporting is slow,” ask: “Which report? Who prepares it? Where does the input come from? How long does preparation take? What decision waits for it?” Do not jump directly to selling a dashboard. Users and adoption “Which roles use the system?” “How do their permissions differ?” “Where do they work?” “What devices and connectivity do they have?” “Who is least comfortable with technology?” “Who will train and support them?” A product for 20 office analysts differs from one for 500 field workers even when both are called a reporting app. Ask what users do when the current process fails. Their workaround may be essential behavior to preserve. A spreadsheet may contain undocumented approval rules that no one mentioned in the brief.

rocess fails. Their workaround may be essential behavior to preserve. A spreadsheet may contain undocumented approval rules that no one mentioned in the brief.  Current system and technology “What happens from the first trigger to completion?” “Which system is authoritative?” “What must connect?” “Who owns access?” “Are there documented APIs and a test environment?” “What data must move?” “What is working well and should stay?” Avoid treating existing systems as failures just because they are old. If the buyer names a preferred technology, ask why: team skill, procurement standard, existing code, performance requirement, or personal preference? Record the reason for the architect rather than arguing from popularity. Team and responsibility “Who will make daily product decisions?” “Who can explain the business rules?” “Who reviews technical work?” “Who accepts the deliverables?” “What can your team provide, and what do you expect us to own?” Unclear ownership is a commercial risk, especially in staff augmentation.

Timing and urgency “What is the target date?” “What business event drives it?” “What happens if it slips?” “Which work must be ready then?” “When do internal approvals and access need to begin?” A deadline tied to a contract or seasonal window is different from a preference. Do not manufacture urgency when the buyer has none. Separate decision date, desired start date, first usable release, and full rollout. The buyer may need a demo in six weeks and production later. Clarifying that can turn an impossible request into a viable plan. To avoid recommending something unsuitable, would an investment in [internally approved range] be clearly out of reach?” Do not invent the range. If the agency has no basis yet, say so and discuss process rather than price. Unknown budget is a gap to investigate, not always an immediate rejection. An approved budget without a valuable problem is also weak qualification. Decision process and competition “Who will use, evaluate, approve, and sign?” “What criteria will you use?” “Is procurement or security review required?” “What other options are you considering, including doing nothing or using your own team?” “What must happen between today and a signed decision?” If the buyer says “I decide,” ask what happens after their approval. Finance, legal, and vendor onboarding may still be on the critical path. If a tender is already specified around another vendor, assess whether participating is worth the cost.

nd vendor onboarding may still be on the critical path. If a tender is already specified around another vendor, assess whether participating is worth the cost.  Risk and success “What would make this project fail even if the software works?” “Which data or functions are sensitive?” “Which third party could block us?” “What was difficult in previous attempts?” “What result after 30 or 90 days would make this a good decision?” Ask who will collect the baseline and outcome data.

Use a loop: ask, pause, reflect, confirm, deepen. Example: “You said supervisors spend two hours checking reports. Is that per supervisor per week?” After confirmation: “What do they check, and which errors matter most?” This is better than accepting the first number and putting it into an ROI slide. Avoid interrupting with a success story before the buyer finishes. Avoid multiple questions in one breath. Write the buyer's exact language where it matters, but distinguish quotation from interpretation. Invite correction: “My understanding is that delayed approval, rather than report creation, is the main issue. Is that accurate?” Watch contradictions. A buyer may say budget is unlimited but refuse any internal sponsor conversation. A deadline may be called urgent without consequences. Explore these respectfully rather than treating confidence as evidence.

Ask about administration, roles, permissions, audit history, notifications, localization, accessibility, exports, data migration, retention, support, monitoring, disaster recovery, licensing, third-party fees, training, and offboarding. These are often missing from screen-based briefs. A “simple marketplace” may need seller onboarding, commissions, disputes, refunds, moderation, payout reconciliation, fraud controls, and tax handling. A “chatbot” may need permission-aware retrieval, evaluation, content ownership, escalation, retention, and operating support. Hidden requirements often determine the real cost.

Framework Meaning Best use and limitation BANT Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline Useful commercial completeness check; weak if used as an interrogation or if budget is still being formed MEDDICC Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion, Competition Useful for complex opportunities; requires real evidence rather than fields filled with guesses MEDDPICC MEDDICC plus Paper process Adds contract/procurement path for complex deals SPICED Situation, Pain, Impact, Critical event, Decision Strong conversation structure for understanding context and urgency CHAMP Challenges, Authority, Money, Prioritization Useful problem-first qualification for service work SPIN Situation, Problem, Implication, Need- payoff Questioning method for developing impact; not a substitute for a buying-process check For a fresher in IT services, use SPICED or CHAMP to guide the conversation, then a short BANT-style commercial check. Add MEDDPICC elements as deal complexity grows. Do not require a junior seller to recite every acronym on a call.

A practical opportunity score Score each dimension 0, 1, or 2: problem evidence, business impact, owner/champion, commercial feasibility, decision path, timing/critical event, technical feasibility, and agency fit. Zero means absent or contradicted; one means plausible but unverified; two means confirmed with evidence. A training threshold of 11/16 can justify further discovery, provided no mandatory blocker exists. It is an internal teaching rule, not a validated prediction model. Mandatory blockers override the score: unauthorized use, impossible critical constraints, unavailable capability, prohibited commercial terms, or an unwillingness to provide essential information. A high score does not automatically justify a fixed quote.

Buyer: We need an app for our field reports. BDE: What happens today from finishing a job to sending the customer the report? Buyer: Technicians send photos on messaging apps. Office staff rebuild a report and finance waits for approval. BDE: Where does the delay usually occur? Buyer: Missing details and supervisor sign-off. BDE: How often does that happen, and what waits on the report? Buyer: Roughly 30 reports a week need chasing. Invoicing can wait several days. BDE: I will record those as estimates until we confirm them. Do technicians need to capture the report without coverage? Buyer: Yes. That was a problem with the last app. BDE: Then offline capture and later sync are important. Who approves the final record, and which finance system receives it? Buyer: A supervisor approves. Finance uses our ERP, but I do not know its API access. BDE: The next useful step is a workflow session with a supervisor and the ERP owner. We can validate approval rules and access, then recommend the smallest first phase. Who would need to approve funding for that assessment? The BDE identified the business chain, qualified an estimate, caught offline behavior, and proposed a concrete next step.

approve funding for that assessment? The BDE identified the business chain, qualified an estimate, caught offline behavior, and proposed a concrete next step.  The BDE did not promise a framework, launch date, or price before feasibility review.

Within the agreed time, send a concise recap: current problem, desired result, confirmed constraints, open questions, and actions with owners/dates. Ask the buyer to correct inaccuracies. Update CRM stage only when its evidence gate is met. Brief the architect before booking technical discovery. Do not send the architect a calendar invitation with “client wants an app” as the entire context. Post-call scoring: Problem depth 20, impact 15, user/system understanding 15, commercial qualification 15, listening 15, summary/next step 10, accuracy and boundaries 10. Pass at 80/100. Fabricated claims, ignored opt-outs, or unauthorized commitments are critical failures requiring retraining.

section_title: Collect constraints without pretending to design
text: Functional requirements describe what the system does. Non-functional requirements describe how well it must work and under which conditions. “Users can submit reports” is functional. “Reports must remain available offline and synchronize safely when a connection returns” adds operating behavior that materially changes design.

section_title: Connect a capability to a result
text: Feature selling describes what you have: “We have React developers.” Solution selling connects components to a need: “We can build your customer portal.” Outcome selling explains the intended business effect: “We can reduce duplicate order entry by connecting the approved portal workflow to your operations system.” The outcome remains a hypothesis until validated. A dedicated team may help reduce a development bottleneck, but adding people can initially slow delivery through onboarding. Explain the mechanism, dependencies, and measurement. Never turn a plausible outcome into a guarantee.

Use five steps: establish a baseline, identify a controllable change, estimate the effect, subtract full costs, and assign a measurement owner. Include alternatives such as process change, configuration, an existing product, internal delivery, or doing nothing. Illustrative example: six coordinators each spend five hours weekly rebuilding reports. At $20 loaded hourly cost and 48 working weeks, the modeled annual effort is $28,800. If a workflow change releases 40% of that time, gross capacity value is $11,520. If annual operating cost is $3,000, modeled annual net value is $8,520 before implementation. An $18,000 implementation has a simple payback of about 25 months under those assumptions. That may be unattractive unless there are additional verified benefits. Do not hide a weak case by adding vague “efficiency” benefits. Ask whether improved billing speed, reduced errors, or new capacity can be measured without double counting. Revenue gain is not the same as profit gain. Use contribution margin when modeling additional sales.

Option Benefit Trade-off Improve the current process Low disruption and cost May not solve system limitations Configure an existing product Faster standard functionality Licensing and workflow constraints Build a narrow custom workflow Fits a valuable specific need Integration and maintenance ownership Build a broad platform Wider control and capability Larger budget, longer learning cycle, more risk Recommend one option with reasons. A consultant can earn trust by saying that custom development is not currently justified. Assignment. Rewrite five service-first statements as problem, mechanism, and measurable-result statements. Reject any claim that cannot identify the baseline, assumptions, or measurement owner.

Effort is the work required. Duration is the calendar time until completion. Five people cannot always complete a five-month job in one month because tasks depend on one another, decisions wait, and coordination costs grow. A senior engineer may cost more per hour but reduce design risk or review time. Job title alone does not prove competence. The BDE collects scope and commercial constraints. Technical leads estimate the work. Delivery checks capacity and sequence. Finance or sales leadership approves rates, margin, and terms. The BDE communicates the approved estimate with its assumptions.

Illustrative USD example for a defined internal portal. The cost rates below are loaded direct delivery costs, not salaries, public market rates, or an agency rate card. Role Hours Direct cost per hour Direct cost Designer 100 $18 $1,800 Frontend developer 240 $22 $5,280 Backend developer 280 $24 $6,720 QA engineer 160 $15 $2,400 Project manager 80 $25 $2,000 Total labor 860 $18,200 Add direct project tools of $800. Base direct cost is $19,000. Add a 15% risk reserve of $2,850 based on identified uncertainty. Risk-adjusted pricing cost is $21,850. The reserve is a pricing allowance, not an accounting expense until incurred. For a target gross margin of 35%, client price = cost divided by (1 minus margin). Here $21,850 / 0.65 = $33,615.38. Round only through the approved commercial process, for example to $33,650. At that price, expected gross profit after the full modeled reserve is $11,800, and modeled margin is about 35.07%. Markup is profit divided by cost. Margin is profit divided by selling price. Multiplying cost by 1.35 gives a 35% markup, not a 35% margin. With a $21,850 cost, that price would be $29,497.50 and margin about 25.93%.

A 10% discount on $33,650 produces a $30,285 price. With the same $21,850 cost, gross profit falls to $8,435 and margin to about 27.85%. Revenue falls 10%, but gross profit falls about 28.5%. Show that effect before approving a discount. A better negotiation may reduce scope, change sequencing, remove an expensive dependency, or adjust approved payment terms. Do not remove essential testing or security just to reach a number. Gross profit is not net profit. Sales cost, management overhead, office expenses, financing, taxes, and other costs still need coverage. Cash collection also differs from revenue. A profitable invoice can still create cash strain if payment arrives late.

T&M: 200 approved hours at $45 = $9,000 invoiced before agreed expenses/taxes. If direct cost is $5,600, gross profit is $3,400 and gross margin is 37.78%. A spending cap limits authorization; it does not imply all backlog items fit. Dedicated capacity: $6,000 monthly revenue less $3,800 modeled direct cost yields $2,200 gross profit, or 36.67% gross margin. Define allocated hours, holidays, leave, replacement, notice, and overtime. Do not silently assume 160 productive billable hours every month. Timeline: The 860-hour portal may require 8 to 10 weeks under a particular team plan, dependency sequence, and client-response assumption. That duration is illustrative and must be validated; total hours divided by headcount is not enough.

An early range supports budgeting. A discovery estimate prices learning. A proposal estimate prices defined work. Mark confidence and assumptions at each stage. Include design, architecture, QA, PM, DevOps, security review, integration, migration, documentation, training, and warranty effort as applicable. Document a scope baseline, client dependencies, estimate expiry, currency, taxes, third-party fees, payment milestones, change rules, and risk reserve. Fixed-price estimates need particular care where requirements or external APIs are uncertain. For India-based agencies selling internationally, ask finance about currency risk, payment fees, tax treatment, withholding, export documentation, and the contracting entity. These are deal-specific professional decisions; do not teach trainees a universal tax answer. Pricing exercise. At $12,000 direct cost, calculate price for 40% margin. Answer: $20,000. At a 10% discount, price becomes $18,000, profit $6,000, margin 33.33%. Explain what assumptions could change the cost before issuing the quote.

section_title: Negotiate trades rather than automatic discounts
text: If the buyer wants a lower price, ask which constraint is fixed: budget, scope, or date. Offer explicit alternatives. A smaller release can preserve quality. A different start date may improve staffing. A longer commitment may change economics only with management approval. Do not invent concessions or exchange discounts for testimonials that could mislead future customers. If the buyer proposes outcome-based fees, confirm a measurable baseline, attribution, access to data, authority over the relevant workflow, and a fair allocation of external risk. A development agency cannot responsibly guarantee the client's sales when it does not control pricing, marketing, or operations.

Use a mutual action plan with steps, buyer and seller owners, due dates, and evidence of completion: solution review, budget approval, security/legal review, procurement, signature, purchase order if needed, payment/start conditions, staffing confirmation, and kickoff. A verbal yes is not a signed deal. A signature may still leave start conditions unmet. At handoff, review the signed scope, assumptions, exclusions, estimate, stakeholder map, acceptance authority, success measures, risks, and every promise made. The delivery lead must accept the handoff. Schedule an early customer check-in to compare delivery reality with expectations. Proposal assignment. Produce a five-to-eight-page proposal for a bounded scenario. Pass only if a buyer can identify what is included, what is excluded, how it is accepted, what it costs, and what must happen next.

An objection may reflect a real constraint, missing information, low priority, or polite refusal. Use acknowledge, clarify, respond, confirm. Do not manipulate discomfort into agreement. chapter_title: AI and the future of IT sales
text: The 2026 McKinsey survey reports that 32% of respondents' organizations had decided against purchasing at least one software product or feature because they could build it internally with agentic coding tools. This is a reported behavior within a survey, not proof that custom agencies or SaaS are disappearing. It does mean buyers may increasingly compare external delivery with AI-assisted internal work. [1] DORA describes AI as amplifying existing organizational strengths and weaknesses. A controlled 2025 METR study found slower completion in a specific setting involving experienced open-source developers using early-2025 tools. Its small sample, task setting, and tool vintage limit generalization. Together these sources argue against quoting a universal productivity multiplier. [2][6] Deloitte's outsourcing research discusses changing combinations of external providers, internal capability, and technology. The commercial implication is to clarify responsibility and demonstrate expertise, not assume every cost-conscious company will outsource. Demand must be validated by segment, geography, and actual buying triggers. [23]

section_title: What may become easier to commoditize
text: Generic brochure websites, standard CRUD interfaces, undifferentiated code production, basic content drafts, and shallow chatbot demos may face more price pressure. This is a directional judgment, not a guaranteed 2030 forecast. Quality, integrations, operating requirements, and market context can keep apparently simple work valuable. Hourly engineering capacity remains useful where buyers need skills and management control. The weaker proposition is selling hours without explaining what those hours achieve. Improve the offer by attaching domain context, accountable work boundaries, validated deliverables, and a credible transition plan. Practical offers to investigate include legacy integration, modernization assessment, data quality, AI evaluation, permission-aware knowledge access, quality engineering, reliability, cloud cost diagnosis, and adoption support. Sell these only when the agency can demonstrate capability and the buyer has a meaningful problem.

After training gates, an illustrative weekly starting range is 15 to 25 researched accounts, 25 to 40 individually reviewed first contacts, and completion of all agreed follow-ups. A manager may set a learning goal of two held discovery conversations per week when lead supply allows. These are capacity hypotheses, not market benchmarks or guaranteed outcomes. Review results after several comparable weeks. If replies are poor, inspect fit, source quality, message, and delivery before increasing volume. If meetings are high but opportunities are weak, inspect qualification. If proposals stall, inspect value, buying process, solution confidence, and competition. More activity at the wrong stage will not fix the constraint.

Monday: review priorities, capacity, and the accounts worth pursuing. Midweek: review one conversation and one research/message sample. Friday: inspect pipeline evidence, stage aging, forecast changes, and losses. Hold a short sales-delivery sync to confirm capacity and recurring scoping problems.
