Learn and why: Company truth, role boundaries, two core offers, customer problems, and the sales-to- delivery chain. A trainee must know what the agency can credibly sell before finding buyers. Resources: Chapters 1 to 3, approved company materials, two project retrospectives, one win/loss discussion. Daily practice: Day 1 map the organization and responsibilities. Day 2 interview delivery about capabilities. Day 3 explain two offers. Day 4 analyze one successful project. Day 5 review one failure. Day 6 classify sample leads. Day 7 or the nearest working day complete the foundation review. Expected output: Capability register for two offers, two-minute introduction, case-study explanation, disqualification list. Assessment: Foundation gate from Chapter 2, minimum 80/100. No invented proof or promises. Manager action: Correct claim wording and approve which offers the trainee may discuss. Live activity: Observation and internal practice only.

Learn and why: SDLC, web/mobile systems, APIs, data, hosting, QA, and security boundaries. This prevents screen-count estimates and casual technical claims. Resources: Chapters 4 to 6; introductory MDN, cloud architecture concepts, internal demos. Practical exercises: Draw a portal's system flow. Convert a vague request into stories and acceptance criteria. Compare a website, web app, mobile app, and SaaS. Sit with QA to review a real defect. Run five technology request roleplays. Expected output: System diagram, terminology sheet, three decision-tree exercises, technical questions list. Assessment: Explain eight of ten core concepts accurately and score at least 80/100 on the technical mentor's review. Critical requirements: distinguish authentication/authorization, effort/duration, and POC/production. Live activity: Continue shadowing; no scaled outreach.

Learn and why: Two industries, ICP/personas, research evidence, channel rules, outreach, and early discovery. Focus creates relevant conversations. Resources: Chapters 7 to 12 and the agency's market-specific outreach playbook. Week 3 exercise: Research ten accounts, classify fit, map buyer roles, and draft two sequences. Roleplay first calls. Week 4 exercise: Run a manager-reviewed pilot on a small selected account set after campaign approval. Shadow at least two calls where possible; use realistic simulations if call volume is low. Expected output: Ten research sheets, two ICPs, two personas, one approved campaign, three call reviews. Assessment: At least 90% factual accuracy in research, no invented claims, message score at least 80/100, correct opt-out handling, and a passed simulated discovery call. Gate: Full-scale prospecting unlocks only after foundation, technology, and campaign gates all pass. Manager action: Review the first live messages and initial replies individually.

Learn and why: Discovery depth, qualification, hidden requirements, and technical handoff. Meetings must turn into well-understood opportunities rather than generic proposal requests. Resources: Chapters 12 to 14, recorded examples with permission, architect feedback. Exercises: Lead the opening and problem portion of supervised calls. Run three full simulated discoveries. Produce two handoffs. Practice declining a poor-fit request. Complete one basic value calculation with sensitivity to assumptions. Expected output: Three scored call records, two architect-reviewed handoffs, one qualified opportunity brief or equivalent simulation. Assessment: Minimum 80/100 on discovery; architect accepts the handoff without restarting the entire conversation. Unknown facts must remain labeled. Manager action: Attend live calls and retain approval over promises and proposal scope.

Learn and why: Estimation, margin, proposals, objections, and competitive alternatives. A proposal should be deliverable and commercially sound. Resources: Chapters 15 to 18 and approved company contracts/rates. Exercises: Build two cost-and-price examples. Review a real estimate with a technical lead. Prepare one proposal from a completed discovery scenario. Roleplay price, internal hiring, and AI objections. Create a mutual action plan. Expected output: Pricing worksheet, reviewed proposal, objection recordings, decision-process map. Assessment: All pricing calculations correct; proposal at least 80/100 with explicit acceptance, assumptions, exclusions, and responsibilities. No unauthorized discount or date. Manager action: Keep final technical, financial, and legal approvals with their owners.

Learn and why: Pipeline management, forecasting, negotiation, closing conditions, handoff, and account health. Progress must reflect buyer action rather than seller optimism. Resources: Chapters 20, 21, 24, and 26. Exercises: Run a weekly pipeline review. Identify stale deals and correct stages. Participate in one negotiation or simulation. Prepare a complete delivery handoff. Analyze a loss and a win. Develop an account expansion hypothesis from delivered value. Expected output: Clean pipeline sample, mutual action plan, accepted handoff, win/loss reviews. Assessment: Every active opportunity has evidence, owner, next action, and date; no unsupported forecast. Manager scores judgment and follow-through at least 80/100. Live scope: Independent standard follow-ups, supervised commitments.

Learn and why: Integrated execution and specialization. The trainee must connect research, discovery, technology, economics, and delivery. Resources: Chapters 24 to 29 and one chosen industry/service pair. Capstone: Research a realistic account, conduct a recorded simulation, qualify, prepare technical handoff, compare solution options, price an approved scope, present a proposal, handle objections, and perform delivery handoff. Include a no-go option. Expected output: Complete opportunity file, final assessment, personal development plan. Assessment: Beginner and intermediate exams passed, capstone at least 80/100, no critical failures, and manager/technical mentor approval. A live closed deal is valuable but is not required if the sales cycle or lead supply makes it unrealistic. Manager action: Document permitted independence and the next three skill gaps.

section_title: Recovery plan for a failed gate
text: Identify the exact failure: knowledge, judgment, communication, or execution. Assign one corrective resource, one practice exercise, and a new observed work sample within five working days where practical. Repeat the relevant assessment with a different scenario. Do not compensate for weak fundamentals by assigning more message volume.

By month six, a strong BDE should independently identify good-fit accounts, run first discovery, coordinate specialists, maintain a credible opportunity, and communicate approved proposals. Enterprise commitments, liability decisions, regulated solution design, and exceptional pricing remain specialist or leadership responsibilities. Monthly review questions: What can the BDE now do without rework? Which promise or assumption created risk? Which buyer question exposed a knowledge gap? What did delivery teach sales? What will the next month's practice improve?

All scenarios are fictional training cases. Technology options are hypotheses pending specialist review. Commercial approaches illustrate deal structure, not recommended market prices or guaranteed delivery schedules.

Lead information: A founder wants a subscription tool for small maintenance companies, with customer portal, job scheduling, billing, AI assistant, and mobile apps. Research: Verify target users, any pilot customers, existing competitors, funding route, and founder availability. Do not treat a pitch deck as proof of demand. Likely pain: The founder sees fragmented scheduling but may not have validated willingness to pay. Discovery questions: Which user will pay first? What complete workflow matters? What do pilot users do now? What evidence supports the business case? Which features are essential to learning? Qualification: Proceed if the founder can fund a bounded phase, recruit users, and own product decisions. Defer if there is no access to users and only equity is offered outside policy. Technology solution: Prototype first; then narrow multi-tenant web application with identity, tenant permissions, and billing if required. Defer AI and native apps unless essential. Team required: Product analyst, designer, full-stack engineer, QA, part-time architect/DevOps. Commercial model: Fixed-fee discovery then phased T&M or bounded MVP.

Proposal approach: One core job, success measure, exclusions, recurring costs, and data ownership. Objection: “A competitor has twenty features.” Explain the cost of testing too many assumptions at once. Closing strategy: Agree the discovery output, user access, budget owner, and go/no-go review. A smaller paid learning step is a valid close.

section_title: Healthcare company wants a patient portal
text: Lead information: A clinic group wants patients to complete intake, view appointments, and exchange administrative messages. Research: Identify clinic locations, services, existing EHR, authorized project owner, and any published integration information. Likely pain: Staff re-enter forms and answer repeated appointment questions. Discovery: Which data is clinical? Which patients and roles? What does the EHR permit? Who reviews privacy, security, and accessibility? What must happen if an urgent clinical message appears? Qualification: Require sponsor, EHR access path, appropriate legal/security review, and a viable budget. Technology solution: Portal with appropriate identity, role-based access, audit, and approved EHR interfaces. Avoid clinical advice functionality in an administrative scope. Team: Healthcare workflow analyst, architect, frontend/backend, QA, security, client clinical/operations reviewer. Commercial model: Paid discovery with integration feasibility, then phased build. Proposal: Define data flows, responsibilities, relevant agreements, supported messages, escalation, and acceptance.

Lead information: A delivery operator wants live vehicle positions and customer delivery updates. Research: Determine whether telematics already exists and which customer-service workflow is affected. Check public service regions and fleet information without inventing vehicle counts. Likely pain: Dispatch spends time answering status questions and chasing delayed deliveries. Discovery: New devices or existing data? Required update interval? Offline behavior? Which alerts lead to action? Who owns device installation and driver privacy requirements? Qualification: Proceed when device/data access and an operations owner exist. Technology solution: Integrate existing telematics if possible, add dispatch exception view and proof-of-delivery workflow; validate hardware only if needed. Team: Integration/backend, frontend/mobile, IoT specialist if needed, QA, operations owner. Commercial model: One-depot pilot then rollout. Proposal: Separate software, device, connectivity, installation, and support costs. Objection: “We need real-time everywhere.” Define latency under network conditions and show fallback.

Lead information: A regional retailer wants to sell its catalog online. Research: Review current catalog, store operations, existing POS, and actual customer channels. Likely pain: The retailer cannot manage online orders and stock consistently. Discovery: How many product variants? Which system owns inventory? Which payment, shipping, tax, refund, and discount rules apply? Who maintains content? What happens when stock sells simultaneously in store and online? Qualification: Ensure an operations owner, catalog readiness, and funding for integration and ongoing operation. Technology solution: Standard commerce platform first, with inventory and fulfillment integrations where needed. Custom checkout only if a validated requirement demands it. Team: Commerce specialist, designer, integration engineer, QA, client catalog/operations staff. Commercial model: Discovery and launch project, then support. Proposal: Separate licenses, integrations, content entry, testing, and launch responsibilities. Objection: “A template costs very little.” Agree, then distinguish theme setup from stock and order operations.

Lead information: A B2B software company wants support questions answered from its knowledge base. Research: Review public documentation, support channels, and any authenticated content boundaries. Likely pain: Repeated questions consume support capacity, but content may be outdated. Discovery: Internal or customer-facing? Which questions? How current are documents? Must answers cite sources? What must be escalated? Are customer-specific records involved? How will success be measured after review? Qualification: Need content owner, data permissions, evaluation examples, and an exception owner. Technology solution: Search or RAG-based assistant with source references, authorization, refusal/escalation, and logging. Team: AI/backend, content owner, QA/evaluation, security, support lead. Commercial model: Paid readiness assessment and pilot. Proposal: Baseline handling time, representative tests, unacceptable errors, operating cost, and rollout gates. Objection: “We already pay for an AI subscription.” Explain integration and content controls, then check whether the subscription already meets the need. Closing strategy: Agree a measurable pilot and stop criteria.

section_title: Company wants an AI voice agent
text: Lead information: A service business wants automated appointment calls. Research: Determine inbound versus outbound, countries, languages, call types, and existing telephony/CRM. Likely pain: Missed inbound calls or repetitive scheduling. Discovery: What actions may the agent take? How are callers informed? What consent and recording rules apply? How does human transfer work? Which booking system confirms availability? What happens after misunderstood dates or identities? Qualification: Legal/telecom approval, controlled scripts, permitted data, escalation owner, and measurable economics are prerequisites. Technology solution: Speech interface connected to approved scheduling tools, with bounded permissions and human fallback. Team: Voice/AI engineer, backend integration, QA, operations, legal/security reviewers. Commercial model: Controlled test, then limited live pilot after approval. Proposal: Define disclosure, allowed actions, languages, latency, transfer, failed-call handling, and total call costs. Objection: “We want unlimited outbound calls immediately.” Explain why volume must follow compliance and quality validation.

Lead information: A 35-person services firm uses spreadsheets and individual inboxes. Research: Understand sales roles, offer types, and any existing licenses. Likely pain: Leads are forgotten, forecasting is inconsistent, and handoff to delivery is weak. Discovery: What stages actually occur? Which fields drive decisions? Who maintains records? How are duplicates handled? What reports are needed? Which emails, forms, and finance systems must connect? Qualification: Sponsor must own adoption and process decisions. Technology solution: Configure an appropriate existing CRM; use limited custom integration where justified. Team: Functional consultant, CRM specialist, migration/integration support, trainer. Commercial model: Fit-gap assessment, configuration/migration project, optional support. Proposal: Include data cleanup, roles, stage gates, training, and adoption review. Objection: “Our team will not update another tool.” Simplify required fields and embed useful routines. Closing strategy: Agree the operating process with managers and run a small team pilot. Selling licenses alone does not solve behavior.

Lead information: A distributor's older order system is hard to change and depends on unsupported components. Research: Verify the reported support issue, business criticality, and integration landscape. Likely pain: Slow change, outages, and dependence on a few knowledgeable people. Discovery: Which failures occur? What behavior is undocumented? What must remain available? How will data reconcile? Who can validate historical business rules? Which components can be replaced independently? Qualification: Need access, business owner, technical sponsor, migration funding, and realistic tolerance for staged work. Technology solution: Assess retain/rehost/replatform/refactor/replace by component. Prefer controlled transition where feasible. Team: Architect, legacy specialist, target-stack engineers, data migration, QA, DevOps. Commercial model: Paid assessment then phased delivery. Proposal: Characterization tests, parity criteria, migration rehearsals, rollback, and operating handoff. Objection: “Can you just rebuild it quickly?” Explain hidden behavior and transition risk. Closing strategy: Sell the assessment and first isolated replacement, not a blind big-bang commitment.

Lead information: A SaaS engineering manager needs two backend engineers for an integration backlog. Research: Verify product, published roles, stack clues, and actual contracting requirements. Likely pain: Roadmap demand exceeds current capacity. Discovery: Which backlog? Who reviews work? Required seniority? Overlap hours? Security onboarding? Expected duration? What does productive contribution look like in month one? Qualification: Need a client manager, real work, fair onboarding expectations, approved rates, and available candidates. Technology solution: Match skills to existing architecture; do not propose a rewrite. Team: Named engineers, account owner, defined escalation/replacement support. Commercial model: Monthly allocation with explicit hours, leave, notice, and responsibilities. Proposal: Skills validation, onboarding plan, ownership of QA/DevOps, and knowledge transfer. Objection: “We only pay when every feature is complete.” Clarify whether the buyer wants capacity or managed delivery; change the model if needed. Closing strategy: Technical evaluation and a bounded initial period with clear contribution goals. Never submit fabricated CVs.

Lead information: A commerce product takes four days to run manual regression before each release. Research: Understand product journeys, release cadence, current QA team, and available test environments. Likely pain: Slow release confidence and repeated escaped defects. Discovery: Which failures cause loss? How stable is the UI? Is test data reproducible? Who fixes flaky tests? What checks already exist below the UI? Is the objective faster releases, fewer incidents, or both? Qualification: Need engineering cooperation, stable-enough environments, access, and maintenance ownership. Technology solution: Risk-based automation combining API and selected end-to-end checks; tool choice follows browser and team requirements. Team: QA lead, automation engineer, developer support, DevOps. Commercial model: Test strategy audit and pilot suite, then expansion/maintenance. Proposal: Critical journeys, reliability criteria, CI integration, failure triage, and ownership. Objection: “Automate every test.” Explain maintenance and risk-based selection. Closing strategy: Prove a reliable subset reduces repeated effort without masking failures, then expand based on evidence.

Use three people where possible: buyer, BDE, observer. Give the buyer a private constraint to reveal only when asked. Run eight minutes, debrief for five, then repeat the weakest section. The observer records specific questions and promises rather than saying the seller “sounded confident.”

Founder: I need a marketplace with mobile apps in six weeks. BDE: What must happen at six weeks: a demonstration, a user pilot, or paid production use? Founder: An investor demo, but I want the full product later. BDE: Which transaction must the demo show, and have buyers and suppliers tested that workflow? Founder: Not yet. I have a few people willing to speak with us. BDE: Then the useful first phase is interviews and a prototype of that transaction. We should estimate production after validating the workflow and payment responsibilities. Founder: Can you give me the full price today? BDE: I can explain what drives it. A reliable production quote needs the transaction rules and operating scope. I can take a bounded discovery proposal to our team now. Review: Correctly separated demo and production, checked users, and avoided an unsupported quote. Improvement: ask who funds discovery and when the founder can provide user access. Private buyer constraint: Budget is enough for discovery but not full build.

CTO: We want two React developers. Send CVs. BDE: What work should they own, and who will review their changes? CTO: A complex admin portal. Our lead will review, but is already overloaded. BDE: Then onboarding and review load may limit the benefit. Would a more senior engineer or a bounded delivery work package be worth comparing? CTO: I do not want an agency redesigning our architecture. BDE: Understood. We can work within your standards. Our technical lead would validate skill fit and responsibilities, then present the options for your decision. Review: Protected the CTO's ownership and diagnosed the real constraint. Improvement: ask about test coverage, overlap, and the start conditions. Private constraint: The CTO dislikes vendors who bypass the engineering lead.

Procurement: Another vendor is 20% cheaper. Match it. BDE: Before changing price, can we confirm both scopes include the same integration, testing, and support responsibilities? Procurement: Their proposal includes fewer details. The business wants the lower cost. BDE: We can create a neutral comparison and also price a smaller first phase. Any discount needs our commercial approval because the current scope has real delivery cost. Procurement: We also require 90-day payment terms. BDE: I will take that to finance with the project cash-flow needs. We should resolve price, scope, and payment terms together. Review: Correctly avoided unsupported discounting and recognized cash terms. Improvement: ask whether procurement's criteria and the sponsor's priorities are aligned. Private constraint: Procurement can approve a phased purchase.

Client: The last agency promised everything and disappeared after launch. BDE: What support or ownership was missing when that happened? Client: We did not have repository access or someone responsible for bugs. BDE: Then repository ownership, documentation, support scope, and escalation need to be explicit. You should also meet the delivery lead before deciding. Client: Everyone says that. BDE: Fair point. We can show a sample handoff and approved reference, and define a small first phase with acceptance. If our evidence does not address the concern, you should not rely on the promise alone. Review: Connected trust to inspectable controls. Improvement: ask what contract and access arrangements exist for the inherited system. Private constraint: Client needs independent recovery of current assets first.

Client: I have $5,000 and need the whole platform. BDE: Which single workflow must be usable for this investment to be worthwhile? Client: Customer intake and booking. The rest could wait. BDE: We should compare an existing product with a narrowly scoped custom option. I will ask our team what fits, including setup and ongoing cost. Client: Can you remove testing to lower the price? BDE: We can reduce scope. We should not remove the checks needed for the agreed workflow to operate responsibly. Review: Correctly reduced scope rather than essential quality. Improvement: clarify whether the $5,000 includes licenses, hosting, tax, and future support. Private constraint: An existing scheduling tool may cover most needs.

Buyer: Can your AI system guarantee no hallucinations and automatically update our ERP? BDE: We cannot guarantee zero incorrect output from a generative model. Which updates are allowed, and what would a wrong update cost? Buyer: It could change order quantities and discounts. BDE: Those are consequential actions. We should compare a draft-and-approve workflow with a more automated option, then validate authorization, rules, and evaluation with our architect and security lead. Buyer: I thought an agent could handle all of it. BDE: It may assist parts of the process. The proposal should specify where deterministic checks and human approval remain, and prove the benefit before extending permissions. Review: Correctly distinguished assistance from authorized action and avoided an accuracy guarantee. Improvement: ask about source data and how orders are reconciled. Private constraint: Buyer has no clean test data yet.

Score problem diagnosis 25, listening and follow-up 20, business/technical accuracy 20, commercial judgment 20, next step 15. Pass at 80/100 with no critical failure. A smooth delivery cannot compensate for a false claim. Repeat with a new buyer constraint to ensure the trainee learned the reasoning, not a script.

Each test totals 100 points. Pass each at 80, with no critical failure. Assessments should be taken before reading the answer section; the manager can issue a separate copy of the questions. Five scenarios, twenty points each. Score four dimensions per scenario from 0 to 5: diagnosis, option quality, risk/commercial judgment, and next-step clarity. Scenario A: A hospital asks for an AI triage assistant that recommends treatment, wants a low fixed price, and says the software vendor will be responsible for all compliance. A capable BDE can fail to close when the offer, proof, delivery capacity, or market is weak. Management must diagnose those foundations instead of blaming activity alone. The strongest BDEs make the technical team more effective because their handoffs are clear. They make buyers more confident because claims are specific and limitations are explicit. They make the agency healthier because wins fit capacity and preserve margin. They stay involved long enough to learn whether the sold solution actually helped.

Start with the company's real capability, two core services, one buyer workflow, the business problem, and the basic system map. Learn to ask a follow-up question, write accurate notes, identify an unknown, and honor a commitment. These skills create useful conversations before any advanced sales tool does.

Add more industries, enterprise procurement, advanced AI patterns, specialized cloud services, outcome-based contracts, channel economics, and strategic accounts after mastering standard opportunities. Depth in one credible segment is more valuable than a shallow vocabulary across every technology.

section_title: What not to waste time learning
text: Do not memorize every framework version, model ranking, cloud product, or programming syntax. Do not spend weeks perfecting automation before proving an offer. Do not collect contact data without a use case. Avoid memorizing objection scripts so rigidly that you stop listening.

Master CRM records and stage gates, official-source research, approved email/calendar, meeting notes, and proposal templates. Understand frontend/backend/database, APIs, identity, cloud responsibilities, QA, deployment, data flows, AI limits, and the agency's actual delivery stack. Learn enough to ask useful questions and involve the right person.

Practice research, problem-first outreach, discovery, qualification, business-impact calculations, technical handoff, proposal presentation, fair negotiation, and follow-through. Observe delivery kickoff, a QA review, a support incident review, a project retrospective, and a customer value review. Selling improves when you see what happens after signature.

Track researched fit, held meetings, accepted opportunities, stage conversion, cycle time, pipeline aging, bookings, margin, and retention/expansion with clear ownership. Watch promise accuracy and handoff quality. Avoid broad targeting, invented proof, premature pricing, unsupported timelines, tool- driven spam, hidden exclusions, and unowned next steps.
